dek: One year after Hurricane Melissa, most rooms are back and winter flights are loaded. Here is how to visit well.

slides.label: The storm
slides.text: On Oct. 28, 2025, Hurricane Melissa made landfall near New Hope, Westmoreland, as a *Category 5*. AccuWeather reports *185 mph* winds at landfall, and NOAA later upgraded its winds over water to 190 mph.

slides.label: One year
slides.text: Last week marked one year. Melissa tied for the *strongest Atlantic hurricane* on record, and the World Meteorological Organization retired the name. AccuWeather reports at least *45 deaths*.

slides.label: The comeback
slides.text: About *90%* of Jamaica's room stock is back, per The Gleaner. Airlines committed more than *1.3 million* winter seats, and more than 80,000 hotel workers are back on the job.

slides.label: The gap
slides.text: Tourism earned about *$2.5 billion* through August, per Open Jaw, but arrivals ran *17% behind* 2025. AccuWeather, citing the AP, says 20 hotels remain closed as peak season begins.

slides.label: Not recovery
slides.text: Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association president O'Brian Heron: *"Reopening is not the same as recovery."* AccuWeather reports *80 public schools* still in tents and on rotation.

slides.label: New York
slides.text: Jamaica is a second home for this city, from the B41 to Gun Hill Road. Tourism is more than *30% of Jamaica's GDP* and roughly *a third of its jobs*, per TravelPulse Canada.

slides.label: Go well
slides.text: Check your specific property, not just the island. Spread money to local cooks, guides and artisans. Book flexible. Tip like you mean it, and be patient with what is *still being fixed*.

slides.label: The Den's take
slides.text: Travel is direct economic solidarity. Hashtags fade; *bookings show up on payroll*. The worst outcome is a diaspora that stays home. Go with eyes open and *respect fully packed*.

caption_instagram:
If you have people in Jamaica, you remember Oct. 28, 2025 by the phone. Last week marked one year since Hurricane Melissa.

Melissa made landfall near New Hope, Westmoreland, as a Category 5, tying for the strongest Atlantic hurricane on record. A year later, about 90% of Jamaica's room stock is back, airlines committed more than 1.3 million winter seats, and more than 80,000 hotel workers are back on the job. Tourism is more than 30% of Jamaica's GDP and roughly a third of its jobs.

The other side: "Reopening is not the same as recovery," says JHTA president O'Brian Heron. Arrivals ran 17% behind 2025, 20 hotels remain closed, 80 public schools are still in tents and on rotation, and AccuWeather reports at least 45 deaths.

caption_linkedin:
One year after Hurricane Melissa, Jamaica's tourism recovery is real but uneven.

About 90% of room stock is operating, airlines committed more than 1.3 million winter seats, and more than 80,000 hotel workers are back. Tourism earned about $2.5 billion through August, yet arrivals ran 17% behind 2025 and 20 hotels remain closed as peak season begins.

The industry itself is drawing the line between reopening and recovery. Some operators funded repairs out of pocket to keep staff employed, and fuel prices, airlift and a proposed tourism tax increase are flagged as risks. With tourism above 30% of GDP, visitor spending that reaches local businesses carries outsized impact.

How should travel brands market a destination that is open but still rebuilding?

By The Innovators Den. Sources: The Gleaner, AccuWeather, Open Jaw, TravelPulse Canada.

title: One Year After Melissa, Jamaica Is Open. It Is Not Finished.
